01.note: The Roman emperor Antoninus, a friend of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, had a daughter named Gira who had sexual relations outside marriage. Too discreet to say so openly, the two talked in plants whose names made puns. Antoninus sent a rocket plant, hinting that she had strayed; Rabbi sent coriander, hinting that she deserved death; Antoninus sent leeks, meaning he would be cut off if he did that; and Rabbi sent back lettuce, meaning: have mercy on her.
01.why: It is one of a run of stories about the secret friendship of Antoninus and Rabbi, told just after the Gemara explains why Rabbi always answered the emperor in coded gestures: he feared that powerful Romans would overhear him.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman emperor who, in Talmudic tradition, was a close and secret friend of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Leader of the Jews of the Land of Israel around 200 CE and editor of the Mishna; often called simply Rabbi.

people.name: Gira
people.about: Antoninus's daughter, whose conduct prompts the exchange.

02.note: Rabbi Yohanan suffered from tzafdina, a disease of the gums and teeth, and went to a gentile noblewoman known as a healer. She treated him on Thursday and Friday, and he asked what he should do on Shabbat, when he could not come. She made him swear not to reveal her remedy, and he swore: 'To the God of Israel I will not reveal it.' She told him the cure, and the next day he went out and taught it publicly.
02.why: The Gemara is asking whether a mouth or gum ailment counts as an internal illness, for which Shabbat may be broken to treat it. Rabbi Yohanan's Shabbat treatment is offered as proof, then set aside because tzafdina spreads to the intestines.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, head of the academy in Tiberias.

terms.meaning: A disease of the gums and teeth that the Gemara says begins in the mouth and spreads to the intestines; its sign is bleeding between the teeth.
A Roman noblewoman; here a non-Jewish woman known as a healer.
The Jewish Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday night, when many kinds of work, including preparing most medicines, are forbidden.

03.note: A non-Jewish slave belonging to Rabbi Levi used to sell hiltit, a pungent spice, and people bought from him because his master was a Sage. When Rabbi Levi died, people came to Rabbi Yohanan and asked whether they could still buy from the slave. He answered that the slave of a haver is like a haver himself, so they could.
03.why: The mishna forbids eating hiltit from a gentile because it is cut with a knife that may carry non-kosher residue. This case shows when it may be bought anyway, and opens a discussion of trusting the household of a careful observer.

people.name: Rabbi Levi
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, whose slave sold spices.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, head of the academy in Tiberias.

terms.meaning: Asafoetida, a sharp-tasting plant resin used as a spice and medicine. It was sliced with a knife, which raised concern about non-kosher residue.
Literally 'associate': a person who has committed to careful observance of the laws of tithes and ritual purity, and whose food could therefore be trusted.

04.note: Ravina was walking with Mar bar Rav Ashi on Shabbat when a corner of Mar's garment, the one holding his ritual fringes, tore. In a second version of the story, Ravina told him on the spot, and Mar asked whether Ravina really expected him to throw his garment off in the street. He explained that human dignity overrides this rule, since the place they were walking was a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden only by rabbinic law.
04.why: The Gemara is asking why Mar bar Rav Ashi would have discarded the torn garment in public, given the teaching that human dignity overrides a prohibition. The answer is that dignity overrides only rabbinic prohibitions, and the second version fits the story to that rule.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage of the fifth century, a colleague of Mar bar Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Babylonian Sage of the fifth century, son of Rav Ashi, the editor of the Talmud.

people.name: Rav bar Shabba
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who explained the human-dignity teaching before Rav Kahana.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Babylonian Sage before whom that explanation was given.

terms.meaning: Tzitzit: the strings the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment. With one torn off, the garment no longer fulfils the commandment and may not be worn into the street on Shabbat.
An area that is neither a private home nor a true public thoroughfare, such as a field or a side street. Carrying there on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.
A verse (Deuteronomy 17:11) telling Israel to follow the rulings of its Sages; the Gemara uses it as shorthand for laws made by the rabbis rather than written in the Torah.

04.flag: The first STORY segment begins mid-sentence, finishing an answer started in the previous segment; the actual event (the torn fringe) is told only in the BEFORE segments.

05.note: When a High Priest died and no successor had yet been appointed, his daily meal offering still had to be brought. At first it was paid for from public Temple funds, as the Torah requires. When the Sages saw the Temple treasury running low, they made the dead priest's heirs pay instead. When they saw the heirs neglecting it, they went back to paying from public funds.
05.why: A mishna lists public payment for this offering as one of seven rabbinic enactments, which seems to make it rabbinic rather than Torah law. Rabbi Abbahu answers that it is Torah law; the Sages changed it and then restored it, which is why it is listed.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel around 300 CE, based in Caesarea.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple in Jerusalem, who brought a special offering of flat cakes of flour and oil every day.
The Temple treasury room, holding funds collected from the whole people to pay for public offerings.
A rule enacted by the Sages, as distinct from one written in the Torah itself.

06.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta was known for testing things for himself. Reading in Proverbs that the ant has 'no chief, overseer, or ruler', he set out to see whether ants really have no king. On a hot summer day he spread his cloak over an ant hole to make shade and marked the one ant that came out. It went back in and told the others shade had come; they all came out, he lifted his cloak, and when the sun hit them they set on the marked ant and killed it. He concluded they had no king, since otherwise they would have needed the king's order to put it to death.
06.why: The Gemara has been describing his experiments with sick hens to test which injuries are fatal, and asks how he earned the title 'researcher of matters'. This story answers, and the Sages then question whether the experiment proves anything.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel around 200 CE, remembered for his experiments with animals.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: A Babylonian Sage of the fourth century who explains the origin of Rabbi Shimon's title.

terms.meaning: A summer month in the Jewish calendar, roughly June to July, the hottest part of the year.

07.note: Rav bar Shabba visited the home of Rav Nahman and was served cooked liver, but would not eat it. The household told Rav Nahman that a Torah student inside, Rav bar Shabba, was not eating. Rav Nahman told them: 'Feed it to Shabba', make him eat it whether he likes it or not.
07.why: The Gemara is discussing whether cooked liver, full of blood, is permitted, and whether its blood spoils other food. Rav Nahman, whose own household poured boiling water on liver, shows here that he regarded such cooked liver as fully permitted.

people.name: Rav bar Shabba
people.about: A Babylonian Torah student who refused to eat cooked liver.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge of the third and fourth centuries, in whose home the meal took place.

08.note: A pious man suffered from pain in his heart, and the doctors said his only cure was to drink warm milk every morning. So a goat was brought and tied to the leg of his bed, and he drank from it. When his friends came to visit and saw the goat, they exclaimed that there was an armed bandit in his house, since goats graze on neighbours' crops. They examined his conduct and found no sin in him except the goat, and on his deathbed he said the same: his only sin was keeping it against the Sages' rule.
08.why: A teaching says the leaders of Israel after Yosef ben Yo'ezer all had some flaw. This story is raised against it: tradition identifies such a 'pious man' as a much later Sage, yet he had no flaw but the goat.

terms.meaning: Sheep and goats. The Sages forbade raising them in settled parts of the Land of Israel because they graze on other people's fields.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

09.note: In the town of Rimon, the slave woman of an olive harvester threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was a boy or a girl. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the priest had not become impure, because martens and hyenas were common there and had probably already dragged the body away.
09.why: The Gemara is testing the rule that a doubt cannot override something certain. Here the baby was certainly thrown in and only doubtfully removed, yet the Sages ruled leniently; the Gemara answers that it was only doubtful the object was a baby at all.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a descendant of Aaron. Priests must avoid impurity from the dead, including being under the same roof as a corpse or leaning over one.
Not carrying the ritual impurity that, in Jewish law, comes from contact with a corpse and bars a person from holy food and places.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

10.note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry the daughter of Rav Hanina. Rav Hanina asked whether the marriage contract should set the wedding for Wednesday, and Ravina agreed. But when Wednesday came, Ravina put the wedding off until the following Wednesday, a full week later.
10.why: Rava has just ruled that a woman who accepts a marriage proposal must wait seven clean days before the wedding, in case the excitement brought on menstrual bleeding. Ravina's delay applies that rule, and the conversation that follows asks whether it covers a young girl too.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, the father of the groom.

people.name: Rav Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose daughter was to marry Ravina's son.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, the document a husband gives his bride setting out his obligations to her; here it also fixed the wedding date.

10.flag: The STORY ends with the unexplained delay; Rav Hanina's question and Ravina's explanation, which complete the episode, are in the AFTER segments.
